newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian PM rejects Asian newspapers attacks.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian PM rejects Asian newspapers attacks.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard lashed out on Tuesday at Asian newspapers critical of his handling of the country's current race debate, saying they had deliberately misrepresented his views.
Asian newspaper editorials in the past few days have said that Howard was pandering to racists in Australia by his refusal to end a debate on immigration that has often been xenophobic.
"They are wrong, they deliberately misrepresent my position, they could not have been written in full knowledge of what I have said," Howard told parliament.
"I have clearly demonstrated that in recent weeks I have denounced intolerance, I have supported a non-discriminatory immigration policy," he said.

Asian newspapers have criticised Howard for not taking a tougher stand in the debate, and especially for not condemning Pauline Hanson, the independent politician who started the six-week national debate.
"Howard's silence endorses Australia's racist fringe", said a headline in Bangkok's The Nation newspaper. The Bangkok Post said: "Howard's position must be clarified".
Asiaweek magazine ran an article on the race debate headlined: "Australia's Fear and Loathing -- Prime Minister Howard must take a stand against racists".

Howard has also come under criticism at home for not distancing himself from Hanson, who complained in her maiden parliamentary speech last month that Australia was being swamped by Asians and called for a halt to immigration.

Howard has said he is opposed to racism and his government's policy of non-discriminatory immigration will continue. But he supports freedom of speech and believes Australians should be able to debate the issue of immigration.
Asians make up about 4.5 percent of the Australian population and account for about one quarter of the 100,000 migrants who enter Australia each year.
Australia ended its White Australia immigration policy, which discriminated against non-whites, in the early 1970s.
